comments.author: @steven-is-an-alien
comments.text:
That's a Sulpher Crested Cockatoo, not any variety of Lorikeet. Sulpher Crested Cockatoos are native to Australia, not Pitcairn. If there is a Cockatoo on Pitcairn, and of the islands, someone brought it there, probably a pet. Your first example are a Bare-eyed Cockatoo and a Goffin's Cockatoo, I think. Neither is a Stephen's Lorikeet. After than you show a Sulpher-crested Cockatoo.

I'm very interested it Pitcairn, and it would be nice if your photos actually represented the location being discussed, and not other places that have Cockatoos.

Personally, I suspect that this is AI generated. I am a huge fan of Artificial Intelligence, with a small AI lab at my home. Althought AI generated content is fantastic, it should still be vetted before being published, lest misinformation propagate, and someone thinks there are Cockatoos on Pitcairn, and who knows what else.

Perhaps train your AI on the your comments, like mine and others. A reasonably designed agentic system should be able to do a much better job. With a proper regimen, you may be able to get your AI to make fewer mistakes than most humans with an interest in the topic. The free-flow and volume of data made possible by AI is potentially a very good thing for humanity, but it's not a terrible idea keep tabs on things until it's so good that a carefully observer can no longer find mistakes, nonsense, and so-called hallucinations..

PS. This is an excellent photo of a Stephen's Lorikeet, endemic, as you say, to Henderson Island:
By James Eaton - https://www.inaturalist.org/photos/395655071, CC0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=159672043


Thanks for considering my input. 🙂


Bottom-line: This video captured me, due to my interest in the topic, and general love of knowledge. Had I not known a great deal about Cockatoos... Hmmmmmmm Something to think about out before delegating to AI, I think. LOL

When the wave hits a steep island, it does not gently roll onto a flat beach. Shallow water usually slows a tsunami down and makes it grow tall. Steep shores mean deep water stays close to the land. The wave keeps its fast speed until it hits the rock wall. The fast wave slams right into the cliff. It shoots water straight up into the air in a giant splash.
